title: Three-Back Sum Sequence
statement:
A sequence starts with s(0) = 0, s(1) = 1 and s(2) = 1. Every later term is the sum of the three terms before it: s(k) = s(k − 1) + s(k − 2) + s(k − 3).

Given n, return s(n).

examples.why: The sequence goes 0, 1, 1, 2, 4. s(3) = 0 + 1 + 1 and s(4) = 1 + 1 + 2.
The first term is given directly.
0, 1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 13, 24, 44, 81, 149. Adding only two terms would give 55 here.

constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer
hints: Write the definition as a recursive function. How many times does it compute s(5) when you ask for s(20)?
Remember each term once you have it, or build the terms from the bottom up in a list.
Each step only needs the last three terms. Keep three variables and slide them forward.

explain.intuition:
The direct recursion branches three ways at every level, so it recomputes the same small terms an exponential number of times. Each term depends only on earlier terms, so compute them in order from the bottom up and each one is computed exactly once.

You never look back further than three terms. So instead of a whole table, keep three variables a, b, c for the last three terms and shift them along, like a sliding window of size three.
steps: Set a = 0, b = 1, c = 1: the terms s(0), s(1), s(2).
Repeat n − 2 times: compute next = a + b + c, then shift a = b, b = c, c = next.
pitfalls: Plain recursion without memory: about 3<sup>n</sup> calls, far too slow for n = 37.
Off-by-one in the loop count. Check it against s(3) = 2 and s(4) = 4.
Starting with 1, 1, 1 or 0, 1, 2 instead of the given 0, 1, 1.

solutions.title: Recursion with memory
solutions.idea: Follow the definition, but store each term the first time it is computed.

solutions.title: Three rolling variables
solutions.idea: Build the terms in order, keeping only the last three.

followups: n can now be up to 10<sup>18</sup> and you need the answer modulo 10<sup>9</sup> + 7. How does a 3×3 matrix power help?
Generalize to summing the previous k terms. Can each step still be O(1) instead of O(k)?
